params.question: Which vascular event in acute inflammation allows protein-rich fluid (>3 g/dL) to escape into the interstitium and form an exudate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vasoconstriction is the very first event and lasts only seconds. It restricts rather than permits protein escape, and does not open the vessel wall.

answers.text: Arteriolar dilation driven by histamine and nitric oxide

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vasodilation increases blood flow and produces redness and heat, but does not by itself allow proteins to cross the vessel wall. Protein escape requires a separate permeability change.

Correct. Mediators such as histamine and leukotrienes cause endothelial cells to contract, widening the gaps between them. This allows protein-rich exudate (>3 g/dL) to escape — unlike a transudate, which forms from hydrostatic or oncotic imbalance without any permeability change.
Stasis follows the permeability increase and slows blood flow, facilitating leucocyte margination. It does not initiate protein leakage — the endothelial contraction step precedes stasis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the vascular sequence: vasoconstriction (seconds) → vasodilation → increased permeability via endothelial contraction → stasis. It is endothelial contraction that opens the vessel wall to protein and produces the exudate.
Well done. Endothelial contraction is the permeability step that defines an exudate; stasis follows, and the cycle ends with leucocyte emigration.

interactions.label: Aspirin blocks the cyclo-oxygenase (COX) pathway but does not inhibit the lipoxy

params.question: Aspirin blocks the cyclo-oxygenase (COX) pathway but does not inhibit the lipoxygenase pathway. Which inflammatory mediator therefore continues to attract neutrophils to a site of infection even after a therapeutic dose of aspirin?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: PGE2 is a COX-pathway product and is suppressed by aspirin. Its main roles are pain sensitisation and fever — not neutrophil chemotaxis.
TXA2 is also a COX-pathway product blocked by aspirin. Its role is vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation, not neutrophil recruitment.

Correct. LTB4 is produced by the lipoxygenase pathway, which aspirin does not inhibit, making it the dominant chemo-attractant for neutrophils that persists despite COX blockade. The cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) from the same pathway increase vascular permeability and cause bronchoconstriction.
PGI2 is a COX-pathway product from endothelial cells that promotes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation. It is suppressed by aspirin and is not a neutrophil attractant.

overallFeedback.feedback: Separate the two arachidonic acid pathways: COX → prostaglandins and thromboxane (blocked by aspirin and NSAIDs); lipoxygenase → leukotrienes (not blocked). LTB4 is the lipoxygenase-derived neutrophil attractant.
Correct. LTB4 from the lipoxygenase pathway escapes aspirin's block, maintaining neutrophil influx even when COX products are suppressed — a key reason NSAIDs alone cannot abolish inflammation.

params.question: A patient receiving a TNF-α inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis develops fever, night sweats, and new upper-lobe pulmonary infiltrates. Which mechanism best explains this complication?

answers.text: TNF-α normally recruits neutrophils via selectin up-regulation; its blockade prevents pus formation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neutrophil recruitment in acute inflammation relies primarily on IL-8 and LTB4, not TNF-α. Selectin expression is part of the general endothelial activation response. TNF-α's critical role in granulomatous disease is sustaining macrophage activation within the granuloma, not directing neutrophil adhesion.

answers.text: TNF-α maintains granuloma integrity by sustaining Th1-driven macrophage activation; its blockade collapses the granuloma and allows mycobacterial reactivation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IFN-γ from Th1 cells drives macrophages into epithelioid cells; TNF-α then maintains this activated state and the structural integrity of the granuloma that contains latent mycobacteria. Removing TNF-α collapses the granuloma scaffold, releasing viable bacilli and causing reactivation.

answers.text: TNF-α drives M2 macrophage polarisation; its blockade impairs repair within the granuloma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: M2 polarisation is driven by IL-4 and IL-13, not TNF-α. TNF-α drives the destructive M1 phenotype and sustains granuloma maintenance — it is not a repair-promoting mediator.

answers.text: TNF-α activates complement C5a, which sustains mast cell degranulation inside the granuloma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: C5a acts on mast cells in the context of acute inflammation, not granuloma maintenance. TNF-α's role in chronic granulomatous inflammation is to sustain Th1-driven epithelioid macrophage activation, not to activate complement.

overallFeedback.feedback: Trace the granuloma circuit: IFN-γ from Th1 cells → M1 macrophage activation → epithelioid histiocytes → TNF-α maintains granuloma structure. Remove TNF-α and the granuloma fails, releasing latent mycobacteria.

Exactly right. TNF-α is the molecular scaffold of the granuloma. This is why screening for latent TB is mandatory before starting any biologic anti-TNF therapy — a direct clinical application of this mechanism.

params.question: A multinucleated giant cell with nuclei scattered randomly throughout its cytoplasm is a Langhans giant cell and indicates tuberculosis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is false. Nuclear arrangement is the distinguishing feature: peripheral horseshoe = Langhans giant cell (tuberculosis, fungi); randomly scattered cytoplasmic nuclei = foreign-body giant cell. Always examine nuclear position at high power when you identify a multinucleated giant cell on a slide.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. Randomly scattered nuclei identify a foreign-body giant cell. Langhans giant cells — characteristic of tuberculosis and fungi — have their nuclei arranged in a peripheral horseshoe or wreath pattern at the cell margin.
